headline: Falkner's Rockpile Porgies Feast While the Current Finds Its Legs
subhead: Sea bass hold tight to structure from the Gulf to Stratford Shoal, stripers go nocturnal, and the neap tide's grip is finally breaking.
body_markdown:
Had a guy on the outer breakwall Tuesday morning hook into a porgy that buried his rod tip so hard I thought he'd snagged a keg. Turned out to be a fat 13-inch scup, mouth full of green crab, and he had four more just like it in the bucket before the tide even turned. That's the kind of week it's been out here — not flashy, but if you know where the rocks sit and you're willing to fish the bottom instead of the surface, there's real reward waiting.

Porgies are thick right now on every piece of structure from the New Haven breakwalls out to Falkner Island. I've been running hi-lo rigs with size 4 hooks, sandworm on one, a chunk of green crab on the other, 2 ounces of lead to hold bottom in 20 to 30 feet. Falkner's outer rockpile has been the standout — anchor up-current on the last two hours of the incoming and let the chum bag do its work. The bite there has been steady enough that I'm not exaggerating when I say limits by 9 a.m. aren't unusual if you're anchored right and the current's moving.

And that current matters more than usual this week. We were dealing with a soft neap cycle that left a lot of these spots barely moving — you'd drop anchor at Stratford Shoal and watch your line hang straight down with no push at all, which is death for porgy and sea bass fishing. We called that one last week, said it'd rebuild as the moon worked back toward full, and sure enough the last few days the flow's come back with some authority. Tuesday's ebb at the Gulf was ripping enough that I had to bump up to 3 ounces just to hold bottom. That's a good problem to have.

Sea bass are riding shotgun with the porgies on every rockpile in the zone. Milford Gulf has been quietly excellent — squid strips on a bucktail teaser rig, dropped tight to the rocks in 25 to 35 feet, outgoing tide. I had a stretch last Thursday where every other drop produced a keeper sea bass in the 14 to 16 inch range, mixed with enough shorts that you had to sort through a few before filling out. Stratford Shoal is holding fish too, but it's deeper and current-dependent — you want the tide moving, not slack, or you're just marking fish on the sounder and watching them ignore you.

Blackfish are off the table for now — CT's summer closure has us locked out until fall, so don't waste bait on tautog jigs out at Charles Island's rockier stretches. Save that program for October.

Stripers are the trickiest piece of the puzzle right now, and that's mostly a water temperature story. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, and New Haven Harbor's been sitting in that same low-70s range — warm enough that the bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal. Daytime, they're holding deep on the edges of the Charles Island sandbar or tucked into the current seams off Stratford Shoal, not doing much. But work that same water after dark on the last two hours of the incoming, drift eels or fish a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig off the bar, and you'll find them willing. Had a report of a mid-20-pound fish taken off the southwest corner of Charles Island around midnight last week on a chunk — that's the program right now, and it should hold as long as this warm, stable stretch of weather doesn't break.

Bluefish are the daytime consolation prize. Bunker pods have been moving along Hammonasset and the flats off Falkner, and when the blues get under them it's a fast, sloppy affair — bucktails, poppers, whatever you've got, just get it in the water before the school moves off. It doesn't last long in any one spot, but it's been reliable enough this week to be worth a look if you're passing through anyway.

Fluke have thinned out on the open flats the way they always do once things heat up — I haven't bothered drifting the shallow stuff off Hammonasset in a couple weeks. Better luck's been in the deeper bends, particularly the channel edges near the Housatonic mouth and the deeper cuts around the Gulf. White Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the last of the outgoing, has been picking through a few keepers mixed with a lot of shorts.

Looking ahead, I like where this is headed. The current's rebuilding as we push toward the full moon in early August, which should sharpen up both the porgy/sea bass bite on the rockpiles and give the striper fishing at night a little more push to work with. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it has been, I'd put my Saturday morning at Falkner's outer pile chasing porgies and sea bass, then swing back for a midnight run at Charles Island if the tide lines up. Watch that moon — bigger swings mean better structure fishing, and that's where this zone earns its keep.
